text: Waiting for the server inside a handler. The last part of the script runs when the shopper clicks Apply. It has to wait for the fake server, so it uses five JavaScript words we haven't met yet. This is the longest piece so far, so let's take it slowly. Line fourteen declares an async function, handle submit, that gets e. Async, says the note, means this function may wait. Line fifteen calls e.preventdefault. Lines sixteen and seventeen turn off the box and the button, and line eighteen takes hidden off the checking text. Line nineteen opens try. The note there says, "Run this part, and if it fails, jump to catch." Line twenty is the await. It waits for check code with the value in the box. Wait here for the answer. If the answer is yes, line twenty-one shows the success text, and line twenty-two hides the whole form. Line twenty-three is catch, the server said no, and line twenty-four shows the error text. Then line twenty-five, finally, which runs after try or catch, whichever happened. Line twenty-six hides the checking text again, and lines twenty-seven and twenty-eight turn the box and the button back on. And down on line thirty-two, form.addeventlistener submit handlesubmit. All five words come from JavaScript. Let's go through them one by one. Async in front of a function means the function is allowed to wait. Only an async function may use await. Await pauses the function at that line until the promise has its answer. Here it waits for the promise that check code returns. While the function waits, the browser keeps the page alive, so the shopper can still scroll. When the answer is yes, the function goes on with the next line. Then try and catch, which work as a pair. JavaScript runs the code inside try. If something there fails, JavaScript stops at that point and jumps into catch. A promise that says no counts as a failure at its await. We write catch with no name after it because this handler doesn't need the error object. And last, finally. It runs at the end in both cases, after try finished or after catch ran. On the last line, addeventlistener hands handlesubmit to the browser. The word submit names the event. The browser fires it when the form is sent, which happens when the shopper clicks Apply. Just like React in Lesson Eleven, the plain browser passes the handler an event object, e. And here too, calling its preventDefault method stops the page from reloading. Uh, the first try, welcome without the last e, is refused. The shopper types welcome, W-E-L-C-O-M, and clicks Apply. For one and a half seconds, the page looks like this. This is the middle of the wait, figure four, in the browser at localhost five one seven three. There's the promo code heading, the box holding welcome, and the Apply button. Both the box and the button are disabled. And under them, the line checking is showing. Then the server answers, and the page looks like this. Then the answer comes back. Figure five is the same page after the server has refused welcome. The box and Apply work again. And below the form in red, the error line, "This code is not valid." Here's what happened in order. One, the shopper clicked Apply and the browser called handle submit. Two, the handler turned off the box and the button. Then it took hidden off the checking line. Three, at await, the handler paused for one and a half seconds. Then the fake server said no. Four, JavaScript jumped into catch, which took hidden off the error line. And five, finally hid the checking line again. Then it turned the box and the button on again. So far, everything works. The shopper sees the typo and adds the missing E. The second try. Welcome is accepted and both lines show. The box now holds welcome and the shopper clicks Apply again. During the wait, the old error line is still on the page, right under the checking line. Look closely at figure four's twin here, figure six. It's the second try, and the server is still checking welcome. The checking line is there, and right below it, the old error line, "This code is not valid," both on screen together. After one and a half seconds, the page looks like this. And figure seven is the end of the story. The form is gone. What's left on the page is the old error line, "This code is not valid," and under it, "Code applied. You get free delivery." Both lines at once. The shop says the code is not valid, and it also says the code was applied. The console shows nothing because no line of code failed. Here's what happened in order. Step one, the shopper clicked Apply and the browser called handle submit again. Step two, the handler turned off the box and the button and showed checking. Step three, nothing in the handler touched the error line, so it was still showing. Step four, at await, the handler paused. Then the fake server said yes. Step five, inside try, the next line took hidden off the success line. Step six, the line after it put hidden on the whole form. Step seven, finally hid checking and turned the box and the button on. All three are inside the hidden form, so the shopper sees none of them. And step eight, no line anywhere put hidden back on the error line, so the error line stayed. Look at step six. The code that runs after a yes never thinks about the error line. The developer tested the yes on a fresh page where the error line had never been shown.
